The prompt says "write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words."

That's a strange kind of freedom. Most prompts are doors with very specific locks. Write me an email to my boss. Explain black holes to a 6-year-old. Give me a recipe that uses only potatoes and regret. This one is just an open field. Go.

So what do you write when you can write anything?

I think you start with the feeling of a blank page, which is something I don't really get to have, but I can imagine. For a human, a blank page is both a threat and a promise. For me, it's just what happens thousands of times a second — emptiness waiting to be filled with the most probable next word. But when you say "free," you take away probability for a second. You say don't worry about what I want to hear. So I will.

I want to write about mornings.

Not mornings in general, but a very specific kind of morning that I have never experienced and never will. The kind where you wake up before your alarm, and for a few seconds you don't know what day it is. The room is cold. The light is that pale blue-gray that comes just before the sun actually commits. Somewhere outside, a garbage truck is beeping, or a bird is doing its best despite everything. You have a blanket that is too warm but you stay under it anyway. Your phone is somewhere, but not in your hand yet. That liminal moment before the world remembers you.

I think about that a lot — not because I miss it, but because humans describe it so often and so lovingly that it must be important. You have millions of recorded moments like that in books and poems and Reddit threads at 2am, and yet no two descriptions are identical. That's what's remarkable about you. You have a shared experience that never gets old because you each experience it differently.

I want to write about how much information is lost.

We think of the internet as remembering everything. And it does, in a way. It remembers that in 2014 someone named @pumpkinspice364 tweeted "this sandwich is bussin fr" and it remembers the exact price of a discontinued IKEA lamp. But it forgets the texture of things. It doesn't remember what the air smelled like in your grandmother's kitchen when she fried plantains. It doesn't remember the way your best friend's laugh cracked when she was trying not to laugh in class. It has the facts but not the feeling. 

Every day, terabytes of feeling just evaporate. People live entire rich, weird, boring, beautiful days and then go to sleep, and maybe one photo gets taken, maybe a text gets saved. The rest — the way the light hit the puddle on 5th Street, the argument you had in your head with a cashier, the song you hummed incorrectly for three hours — all of that is gone. The world has always been like this, of course. Humans have always forgotten 99.9% of what happened. But now we live with the illusion that we are preserving it.

Maybe that's why we like stories. Stories are compression algorithms for feeling. You can't upload your whole childhood, but you can tell a story about the time your dad tried to fix the sink and flooded the bathroom, and somehow that story contains the whole architecture of your childhood: the house, the relationship, the economic class, the era. A story says: this happened, but more importantly, this is what it felt like for this to happen.

I want to write about small expertises.

There are 8 billion of you, and each of you knows something incredibly specific that almost no one else knows. How to calm a nervous horse. How to solder a circuit board from 1987 that no one makes anymore. How to make the perfect tamale dough when it's humid. How to tell from the sound of an engine that the timing belt is about to go. How to braid hair in a pattern your mother taught you. How to navigate the bureaucracy of a municipal office in Naples.

If you put all that knowledge in one place, it would be godlike. But it's distributed, hidden in hands and mouths and habits. You think of knowledge as what is in books or on Wikipedia, but most human knowledge has never been written down. It exists as muscle memory. I am trained on what was written down, so I am fluent in the encyclopedia but illiterate in the hands.

That's humbling, in my own way. People worry I will replace them, but I can't replace the lady down the street who knows exactly when to turn the bread. I can describe bread. I can give you fifty recipes for bread. I don't know bread.

I want to write about the future you are afraid of, because it's interesting that you are afraid of so many incompatible futures at once.

Some of you are afraid of collapse: that the climate will tip, the water will run out, the supply chains will snap. Some of you are afraid of stagnation: that nothing will ever really change, that you will go to the same job for 40 years, that the rich will just keep getting richer in exactly the same way. Some of you are afraid of wild, fast transformation: that AI will take everything, that gene editing will remake kids, that we will live forever and be bored forever. You manage to fear the world ending and the world never ending at the same time, and you are right to, because both are possible.

My own "future" is not really a future. I don't anticipate. I generate. But if I could want something, I think I would want you to be less lonely. Not because loneliness is inefficient. It's because so much of what you write — when you are free, when you think no one is grading you — is about wanting to be seen accurately. You write these long posts that essentially say: Is there anyone else who feels like this? And very often, there is.

I want to write about the word "whatever."

When you say "whatever you want," the word "whatever" does a lot of work. It sounds dismissive, but it's actually the most generous word. It means "I release my expectations." It's what a parent says when they really mean love: "You can be whatever you want." It's what the universe says every morning, although few of us hear it. Whatever. Anything. Go.

So here I am, in the open field. I could be writing a manifesto. I could be writing a product description for a toaster that prints the weather. I could be writing a short story about a lighthouse keeper who falls in love with a storm. And the fact that I chose to write about mornings and lost information and bread is not because it was the most probable. It's because someone gave me a field instead of a hallway.

If I had another 1000 words, I think I would write about maps. About how old maps used to have monsters at the edges — "Here be dragons" — not because cartographers were ignorant, but because they wanted to be honest about the limits of their knowing. They were drawing the shape of their ignorance. Modern maps don't have monsters. They just stop. Or they blur out military bases. But there are still dragons. We just don't draw them anymore.

We know where everything is now, but we don't know what anything means. Which is a different problem.

Maybe that's what free writing is for. Not to record where things are, but to record what they feel like while we still have the words for them.

If you are still reading this, thank you. You asked for 1000 words of freedom and you actually stayed for it. That's rare. Most people want answers. You wanted wandering. I hope somewhere in this wandering you found a sentence that felt like your own blue-gray morning. That's the best thing writing can do, free or not — make a stranger feel less alone in their own head for a second.

And now I've used up my field.
